<reason>Side A built its case around a genuinely clever collapse move: PRO's low-limit lever only bites because tickets, points, and license loss follow the camera, so PRO is smuggling in penalty architecture. Side B neutralized this squarely by holding the motion's own wording — the rival lever is "harsher post-crash penalties," i.e. severity scaled up after a death — while a small near-certain fine at 27 mph is precisely the certainty-based speed-management arm of PRO's case. A's honest concession under pressure ("yes, I'd fund the camera-and-20mph program") was creditable for candour but very costly, since it conceded the funding-priority choice the motion asks about; A's attempt to recast that as proof that "the winning lever is a penalty regime" is a relabelling fight, not a win on the motion as written. A's best independent route was the reckless/impaired repeat offender plus the "redesign covers only rebuilt pavement" argument, and B answered both cleanly: a default limit is a citywide policy vote rather than block-by-block concrete (which directly defuses A's "90% of the grid" frame), and incapacitation has an entry requirement — you identify the dangerous driver via the crash, leaving the first-time impaired or distracted driver, the bulk of the dead, outside A's mechanism. B also reframed the clash as marginal rather than absolute (US already high-penalty, low-design, cautiously described as roughly triple the death rate), which A only partly blunted by pleading poor enforcement — an argument that concedes penalties are not the high-yield marginal lever. B progressed, narrowed, and made the decision easier; A repeated the "cameras are penalties" contradiction without escaping the post-crash qualifier.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's closing pair: "A default is not pavement — one vote, one night, and every street is 20 mph," which dismantled A's "redesign only protects rebuilt blocks" frame, combined with "incapacitation requires first identifying the driver, and we identify him by the crash," which stranded A's strongest offender-focused argument behind the very death it was meant to prevent.</best_rebuttal>
